title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation:  Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning regression and classification tools typically do not capture model uncertainty, whereas Bayesian models do but at prohibitive computational cost. The paper casts dropout training in neural networks as approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: averaging T stochastic forward passes to estimate predictive mean and variance. On UCI regression benchmarks, notably Boston Housing, MC dropout improves test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and probabilistic back-propagation, achieving 2.97 ± 0.19 RMSE on Boston Housing in the 20-split setting.

text: Cloning into 'repo'...

why: The authors' repo is cloned and contains the entire experimental apparatus: experiment.py, net/net.py, and all UCI_Datasets directories with data.txt, the exact 20 train/test index splits, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs/n_hidden configs, plus the authors' published result files (test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt etc.) for direct comparison. Nothing data- or weight-wise is missing (models are trained from scratch). What is broken is the runtime: the code targets Keras 2.2.0 on Theano 0.8.2 (README), Theano is unmaintained and not installable on Python 3.12, TF1.x/Keras 2.2 wheels do not exist for Python 3.12, and 9 of 11 Python files are Python-2 style. So we keep the authors' logic (architecture, dropout rates, epochs, tau/grid-search protocol, per-split train/val selection) but port the training/evaluation core to a modern framework and run the same splits.
est_runtime: Port work: ~20-30 min (rewrite net/net.py + experiment.py training/MC-dropout loop in a modern framework, keep split loading and grid-search logic). Runs (Boston Housing, 1x50 net, 400 epochs, batch 32, per-split grid over the repo's dropout_rates/tau_values, T MC forward passes): ~10-15 s per model fit on 22 CPU cores, so ~2-4 min per split with grid search. Full 20-split C1 protocol is ~40-80 min of compute, i.e. borderline-to-over the ~60 min total budget once the port is included.
scale_down_plan: Keep the exact released protocol but shrink along the split axis, not the model axis: evaluate the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits (index_train_*/index_test_*), same 1-hidden-layer/50-unit net, same dropout rates, same l=1e-2, same per-split train/val grid over tau, same 10x epochs (400), batch 32, Adam, T MC forward passes. Report mean test RMSE with standard error over 5 splits and state the split count explicitly. Secondary cheap confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308, <1 min/split) if time permits. Expected effect on the number: the point estimate should land near the released 2.83-2.97 range within a much wider error bar (SE roughly sqrt(20/5)~2x larger, i.e. +/-0.3-0.4 instead of +/-0.19); the qualitative claim (MC dropout beats VI, comparable-to-better than PBP 3.01) remains testable, but the printed +/-0.19 cannot be matched with 5 splits. If the port finishes fast, extend toward 10-20 splits; do not cut epochs or MC samples first, since those change the estimator itself.
blockers: code targets Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 2.2.0; Theano is dead and cannot be installed on Python 3.12
Keras 2.2.0 / TensorFlow 1.x have no wheels for Python 3.12 (and Keras 3 API differs: layer-level train-time dropout loops, .compile/.fit behaviour, model saving)
9 of 11 python files are Python-2 style (print statements, old import style) and need 2to3-style edits even before framework porting
no GPU on this machine; README launch command assumes device=gpu + float32 (not fatal: the UCI nets are tiny and the paper reports CPU-class runtimes, e.g. naval 276 s/split incl. BO)
protocol requires a per-split train/val split + grid search over dropout rate and tau before the final train, so per-split cost is much larger than a single 400-epoch fit

approach: This is a partial_release reproduction: we keep the authors' released data and the exact 20 per-split train/test index files from https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps (bostonHousing/data/data.txt, index_train_i.txt, index_test_i.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt) and their grid-search-over-dropout-rate-and-tau protocol, but re-implement the 1-hidden-layer/50-unit dropout network plus the MC-dropout training/evaluation loop in PyTorch (CPU) because the original Keras 2.2.0 + Theano 0.8.2 stack and its Python-2 source cannot run on Python 3.12 (this is the single documented deviation from R13). For each of the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits we carve an 80/20 train/validation split from the training indices, grid-search dropout rate and tau by validation log-likelihood, set the L2 weight decay from the searched tau and l=1e-2 via the eq.(7) relation exactly as coded in net/net.py, train the final model for the fixed epoch budget (10x the base schedule, ~400 epochs, no early stopping) with Adam/batch-32, and evaluate test RMSE (inverse-transformed to original target units) and predictive log-likelihood with T=1000 MC-dropout stochastic forward passes. reproduce.py aggregates mean±standard-error over the 5 splits, writes results/metrics.json, and prints the authors' released per-split result files for direct comparison. The expected point estimate is ~2.83-2.97 (inside the 0.19 tolerance around C1=2.97) but with a roughly 2x wider standard error (5 of 20 splits), so the honest verdict is partially_reproduced.
steps: 1. Environment: verify python>=3.12, numpy/scipy/pandas/scikit-learn present, then `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` (CPU wheel) and `python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__)"`. Do NOT attempt to install Theano/Keras 2.2/TF1 - they are uninstallable on 3.12 (documented blocker; deviation from R13).

2. Repo check: confirm DropoutUncertaintyExps/ is present; assert existence of UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/data/{data.txt, index_features.txt, index_target.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt, n_splits.txt} and index_train_0..19.txt / index_test_0..19.txt, plus results/ releasing test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt.

3. Read experiment.py and net/net.py end-to-end; write down (in a notes file or docstring) the exact protocol: how the 80/20 train-val split is formed, how (dropout_rate, tau) are grid-searched and scored, how weight decay lambda is derived from tau/l/N, the exact epoch count and multiplier, and how RMSE and eq.(8) log-likelihood are computed. This dictation of the authors' logic is what the PyTorch port must mirror.
4. Parse the bostonHousing data dir config files and print them (dropout rates, tau values, n_epochs, n_hidden, n_splits, index_features, index_target) so the counts drive the grid size.
5. Write config.py with the values above (paper/assumption tags inline).
6. Write data_utils.py: load_data(split) -> (X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test, scaler_y); standardize X and y on train statistics; verbose shapes. No torch import needed here.
7. Write model.py: DropoutRegressor(Q, hidden=50, p_in, p_out) with dropout before each weight layer; keep_dropout_at_eval flag.

8. Write mc_dropout.py: compute_lambda(tau,l,N) reading net/net.py's formula; train_model(...) (Adam lr=1e-3, batch 32, fixed epochs, shuffled); mc_predict(model, X, T=1000) -> mean, variance; rmse_inverse(y, yhat_mean, scaler_y); predictive_log_likelihood(...) per eq.(8)/net.py; grid_search(...) scoring by validation LL.

9. Write reproduce.py: iterate config.full_split_list, run grid search then final train then MC test eval, store per-split results, compute mean and SE = std/sqrt(n), set within_tolerance = |mean - 2.97| <= 0.19, dump results/metrics.json including split count, config snapshot, and the authors' released values.
10. Write compare_with_released.py to read the authors' results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt files and print alongside ours.
11. Run the intermediate checks (see intermediate_checks) and fix any that fail before the full run.
12. Smoke test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` (split 0, 2 epochs, T=10, 1 grid point, 64 samples) - assert finite RMSE/LL, correct tensor shapes, <60 s.
13. Full run: `python reproduce.py --dataset bostonHousing --split-count 5` -> 5 splits x (grid search + 10x-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval).
14. Inspect results/metrics.json: mean RMSE vs 2.97 with tolerance 0.19; compare to the authors' released 2.83/2.90; confirm the printed SE is ~2x the paper's because only 5 of 20 splits are used.
15. If budget remains after the 5-split Boston run, add a cheap secondary confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308), same protocol, and append it to metrics.json.

16. Write a short summary block into results/metrics.json stating the deviation (5/20 splits, grid-search instead of BO, PyTorch instead of Keras/Theano) and the resulting verdict (partially_reproduced).
smoke_test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` runs only split 0 on the first 64 training rows for 2 epochs with T=10 MC forward passes and a single (dropout,tau) grid point; it asserts the data loader returns correctly shaped train/val/test arrays, the net has 751 parameters, training losses are finite and decreasing, MC predictions have shape (n_test,) with non-negative variance, and RMSE/log-likelihood are finite scalars. It writes results/smoke_metrics.json and must finish in under ~60 s, proving the full data->train->MC-eval->JSON flow before the expensive run.
intermediate_checks: Data integrity: data.txt has 506 rows and Q columns equal to index_features.txt; index_train_i.txt and index_test_i.txt are disjoint and their union is all 506 indices; every index is in range.
Split hygiene: the 80/20 validation set is drawn only from training indices, disjoint from the test indices, and reproducible from the fixed seed (A3/A8).
Grid files parse: dropout_rates.txt and tau_values.txt yield the expected number of values (print them); grid size = len(rates)*len(taus).
Parameter count: 13*50+50 + 50*1+1 = 751 parameters; print and assert this matches the instantiated model.

Weight-decay sanity: print lambda for the searched tau values and N=train size; assert lambda > 0 and varies monotonically with tau as eq.(7)/net.py implies; verify lambda matches net/net.py's formula on a hand-computed example.
Target scaling: after standardization the train target has mean~0, std~1; inverse_transform(standardize(y))==y within 1e-8.

Sanity baseline: fit a plain (dropout-off at eval, or a least-squares linear) model on split 0 and confirm test RMSE is in a plausible Boston range (~3-6), i.e. the pipeline is not degenerate before the dropout run.

Authors' anchor: read UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/results/test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt and record the released per-split RMSEs (expect point estimate ~2.83-2.97) so our numbers can be compared immediately after the full run.
budget_plan: Total ~60 min. Setup + reading experiment.py/net.py + writing the PyTorch port: ~15-20 min. Intermediate checks: ~5 min. Smoke test: ~1-2 min. Full 5-split Boston Housing run (grid search + 400-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval, ~2-4 min/split on the CPU cores): ~10-20 min. Aggregation, comparison to released files, and writing results/metrics.json: ~5 min. Remaining ~5-10 min reserved as buffer; if the port finished fast and the buffer is intact, extend the split list toward 10 before considering any reduction of epochs or T (the route forbids shrinking the estimator).

    2|

    4| We replaced the Bayesian optimisation implementation (which was used to find hypers) with a grid-search over the hypers. This is following feedback from @capybaralet who spotted test-set contamination (some train-set points, used to tune hypers which were shared across all splits, were used as test-set points in later splits). The new implementation iterates over the 20 splits, and for each train-
    5| 
    6| Below we report the new results using grid-search (_new_, with code in this updated repo) vs. results obtained from a re-run of the original code used in the paper which used Bayesian optimisation (_paper_, code in [previous commit](https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps/tree/a6259f1db8f5d3e2d743f88ecbde425a07b12445)). Note that we report slightly different numbers for _paper_ than in 
    7|

The baseline experiment (_paper_) was to simply run the previous "10x epochs one layer" code (can be found [here](https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps/tree/a6259f1db8f5d3e2d743f88ecbde425a07b12445)) with the new versions of Theano and Keras. 
    9| The new code (_new_) uses 10x training epochs and one layer as well, and trains models on the same 20 randomly generated train-test splits of the data. Each training set is further divided into an 80-20 train-validation split to find best hyperparameters, dropout rate and tau value through grid search. """Configuration for the reproduction of Table 1 (Boston Housing, MC dropout).

Every value is annotated with the paper requirement id (R*) it satisfies or the
assumption id (A*) recorded in state/assumption_ledger.json.

The authoritative protocol source is the authors' released code
(repo/experiment.py + repo/net/net.py); where the paper text and the released
code disagree, the choice is recorded explicitly below.
"""

import os

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Paths
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
REPO_ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
AUTHORS_REPO = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "repo")
UCI_ROOT = os.path.join(AUTHORS_REPO, "UCI_Datasets")

RESULTS_DIR = os.path.join(REPO_ROOT, "results")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset (R11: UCI regression datasets, N and Q as in Table 1)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
DATASET = "bostonHousing"          # N=506, Q=13 (Table 1)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Network architecture (R1: one hidden layer of 50 units)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
N_HIDDEN_LAYERS = 1                # R1 / data/n_hidden.txt (=50 units, 1 layer)
N_HIDDEN_UNITS = 50                # R1 / data/n_hidden.txt
ACTIVATION = "relu"                # A1 (paper does not state the nonlinearity)

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dropout (R2: dropout before every weight layer)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The released net/net.py applies ONE dropout rate (taken from the grid-search
# file data/dropout_rates.txt) before every weight layer.  The paper text says
# "dropout with probabilities 0.05 and 0.005"; both of those values are members
# of the released grid, and the released grid is what the authors actually ran.
DROPOUT_RATES_FILE = "dropout_rates.txt"
TAU_VALUES_FILE = "tau_values.txt"

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Prior / weight decay (R3, R7, eq. (7) as implemented in net/net.py)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
LENGTHSCALE = 1e-2                 # R7: prior length-scale l = 1e-2
# lambda = l^2 * (1 - p_dropout) / (2 * N * tau)   (net/net.py line 72)
# This is eq. (4)'s regulariser p_i*l^2/(2*tau*N)*||M_i||^2 with p_i the
# *keep* probability; eq. (7) is the p=1 special case.  See A20.

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Optimisation (R5, R6, R12)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
N_EPOCHS_BASE = 40                 # data/n_epochs.txt (PBP's 40 epochs)
EPOCH_MULTIPLIER = 10              # R5: 10x more epochs than the 40-iteration
                                   # BO schedule -> 400 epochs (Table 1).
                                   # (The shipped *_100_xepochs_* files are the
                                   # Table-2 / 100x-PBP setting = 4000 epochs.)
BATCH_SIZE = 32                    # R6 (paper).  NOTE: released net/net.py uses
                                   # 128; deviation recorded in A16.
ADAM_LR = 1e-3                     # A6 (Keras/PyTorch Adam default)
ADAM_BETAS = (0.9, 0.999)
ADAM_EPS = 1e-8
SHUFFLE_EPOCHS = True              # A11 (Keras fit(shuffle=True) default)
EARLY_STOPPING = False             # R12

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Monte-Carlo dropout evaluation (R8, R9)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
T_TEST = 10000                     # A21: authors' net.py uses T = 10000
T_GRID = 1000                      # A21: cheaper T while grid-searching
MC_CHUNK = 500                     # rows of the (T x n) expansion per forward

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Splits (R10)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
N_SPLITS_FILE = "n_splits.txt"
DEFAULT_N_SPLITS = 5               # A19: scale-down along the split axis only
FULL_SPLIT_LIST = list(range(20))  # R10 (paper): 20 random splits

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reproducibility
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
SEED = 1                           # A12: fixed seed (experiment.py uses
                                   # np.random.seed(1)); the released code does
                                   # not seed the weight initialisation, so the
                                   # seed only makes *our* run reproducible.

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Smoke-test overrides
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
SMOKE = dict(
    n_splits=1,
    n_epochs=2,
    t_test=10,
    t_grid=10,
    max_train_rows=64,
    grid_dropout_rates=[0.05],
    grid_tau_values=[0.1],
)


def dataset_paths(dataset=DATASET):
    """Return the dict of file paths for one UCI dataset directory."""
    d = os.path.join(UCI_ROOT, dataset, "data")
    r = os.path.join(UCI_ROOT, dataset, "results")
    return dict(
        data_dir=d,
        results_dir=r,
        data_file=os.path.join(d, "data.txt"),
        dropout_rates=os.path.join(d, DROPOUT_RATES_FILE),
        tau_values=os.path.join(d, TAU_VALUES_FILE),
        n_hidden=os.path.join(d, "n_hidden.txt"),
        n_epochs=os.path.join(d, "n_epochs.txt"),
        n_splits=os.path.join(d, N_SPLITS_FILE),
        index_features=os.path.join(d, "index_features.txt"),
        index_target=os.path.join(d, "index_target.txt"),
        index_train=lambda i: os.path.join(d, "index_train_%d.txt" % i),
        index_test=lambda i: os.path.join(d, "index_test_%d.txt" % i),
    )

"""Data loading for the UCI regression benchmarks, mirroring repo/experiment.py.

Protocol (from the authors' released experiment.py):
  * data.txt holds [features..., target]; columns are selected with
    index_features.txt / index_target.txt.
  * index_train_i.txt / index_test_i.txt give the 90/10 train/test split for
    split i (Boston: 455 train / 51 test).
  * The training block is further carved deterministically into 80/20
    train/validation:  n_tr = int(0.8 * n_train);  val = rows[n_tr:].
  * Inputs are standardised with the mean/std of the *fitting* training block;
    the target is standardised with the mean/std of the same block
    (net/net.py `normalize=True`).
"""

import numpy as np

import config


def _as_list(path):
    return np.loadtxt(path).tolist()


def load_dataset_config(dataset=None):
    """Read the hyper-parameter / split files shipped with the dataset."""
    p = config.dataset_paths(dataset)
    cfg = dict(
        dropout_rates=_as_list(p["dropout_rates"]),
        tau_values=_as_list(p["tau_values"]),
        n_hidden=int(np.loadtxt(p["n_hidden"])),
        n_epochs=int(np.loadtxt(p["n_epochs"])),
        n_splits=int(np.loadtxt(p["n_splits"])),
        index_features=[int(i) for i in np.loadtxt(p["index_features"]).tolist()],
        index_target=int(np.loadtxt(p["index_target"])),
    )
    return cfg


def load_raw(dataset=None):
    """Return (X, y) for the whole dataset with the shipped column selection."""
    p = config.dataset_paths(dataset)
    data = np.loadtxt(p["data_file"])
    index_features = [int(i) for i in np.loadtxt(p["index_features"]).tolist()]
    index_target = int(np.loadtxt(p["index_target"]))
    X = data[:, index_features]
    y = data[:, index_target]
    return X, y


def load_split(dataset, split):
    """Return (index_train, index_test) as integer arrays for one split."""
    p = config.dataset_paths(dataset)
    index_train = np.loadtxt(p["index_train"](split)).astype(int).ravel()
    index_test = np.loadtxt(p["index_test"](split)).astype(int).ravel()
    return index_train, index_test


class TargetScaler(object):
    """Standardisation of the target, exactly as net/net.py does it."""

    def __init__(self, y):
        y = np.asarray(y, dtype=np.float64).ravel()
        self.mean = float(np.mean(y))
        self.std = float(np.std(y))          # ddof = 0, as np.std
        if self.std == 0:
            self.std = 1.0

    def transform(self, y):
        return (np.asarray(y, dtype=np.float64) - self.mean) / self.std

    def inverse_transform(self, y):
        return np.asarray(y, dtype=np.float64) * self.std + self.mean


class FeatureScaler(object):
    """Standardisation of the inputs, exactly as net/net.py does it."""

    def __init__(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
        self.std = np.std(X, 0)
        self.std[self.std == 0] = 1.0
        self.mean = np.mean(X, 0)

    def transform(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
        return (X - np.full(X.shape, self.mean)) / np.full(X.shape, self.std)


def make_split(dataset, split, val_fraction=0.2, verbose=False):
    """Build the train / validation / test tensors for one released split.

    Returns a dict with numpy arrays.  Targets are returned BOTH in original
    units (``*_orig``) and standardised (``*_std``); the scalers are returned so
    that predictions can be mapped back to the original units for the RMSE.
    """
    X, y = load_raw(dataset)
    index_train, index_test = load_split(dataset, split)

    X_train_all = X[index_train]
    y_train_all = y[index_train]
    X_test = X[index_test]
    y_test = y[index_test]

    # Deterministic 80/20 carve of the training block (experiment.py lines
    # 132-136): the LAST 20% of the training rows become the validation set.
    n_fit = int((1.0 - val_fraction) * X_train_all.shape[0])
    X_fit, y_fit = X_train_all[:n_fit], y_train_all[:n_fit]
    X_val, y_val = X_train_all[n_fit:], y_train_all[n_fit:]

    # Scalers are fitted on the block that is actually trained on.
    fs_fit = FeatureScaler(X_fit)
    ts_fit = TargetScaler(y_fit)
    fs_all = FeatureScaler(X_train_all)
    ts_all = TargetScaler(y_train_all)

    out = dict(
        split=split,
        # grid-search phase: fit on 80% of train, validate on the other 20%
        X_fit=fs_fit.transform(X_fit), y_fit=ts_fit.transform(y_fit),
        X_val=fs_val_transform(X_val, fs_fit), y_val=y_val,
        y_val_std=ts_fit.transform(y_val),
        # final phase: fit on 100% of train, test on the released test block
        X_train_all=fs_all.transform(X_train_all),
        y_train_all=ts_all.transform(y_train_all),
        X_test=fs_all.transform(X_test), y_test=y_test,
        y_test_std=ts_all.transform(y_test),
        scaler_y_fit=ts_fit, scaler_y_all=ts_all,
        n_train_total=int(X_train_all.shape[0]),
        n_fit=int(X_fit.shape[0]), n_val=int(X_val.shape[0]),
        n_test=int(X_test.shape[0]),
    )
    if verbose:
        print("split %d: fit=%d val=%d train_all=%d test=%d (Q=%d)" % (
            split, out["n_fit"], out["n_val"], out["n_train_total"],
            out["n_test"], X.shape[1]))
    return out


def X_val_transform(X_val, fs):
    return fs.transform(X_val)

"""The Table-1 regression network, ported from repo/net/net.py to PyTorch.

Authors' Keras 2.2 graph (net/net.py lines 74-82), for n_hidden = [50]:

    inputs  = Input(shape=(Q,))
    inter   = Dropout(p, training=True)(inputs)          # dropout BEFORE layer 1
    inter   = Dense(50, activation='relu', W_regularizer=l2(reg))(inter)
    inter   = Dropout(p, training=True)(inter)           # dropout BEFORE layer 2
    outputs = Dense(1, W_regularizer=l2(reg))(inter)

so dropout is applied before *every* weight layer (R2), the hidden layer is
ReLU (A1) and the output layer is linear.  Keras 2.2 defaults are reproduced:
Glorot-uniform kernels, zero biases, and the l2 regulariser adds
``reg * sum(w**2)`` to the (batch-mean) MSE loss.
"""

import math

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.init as init


def glorot_uniform_(w):
    """Keras 2.2 Dense default kernel initialiser (fan_in/fan_out Glorot)."""
    fan_in, fan_out = init._calculate_fan_in_and_fan_out(w)
    limit = math.sqrt(6.0 / (fan_in + fan_out))
    init.uniform_(w, -limit, limit)


class DropoutRegressor(nn.Module):
    """1-hidden-layer dropout regressor with dropout forced ON at test time."""

    def __init__(self, n_features, n_hidden=50, dropout=0.05, n_hidden_layers=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_features = n_features
        self.n_hidden = n_hidden
        self.dropout_p = float(dropout)
        self.n_hidden_layers = n_hidden_layers

        layers = []
        in_dim = n_features
        for _ in range(n_hidden_layers):
            layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, n_hidden))
            in_dim = n_hidden
        self.hidden_layers = nn.ModuleList(layers)
        self.output_layer = nn.Linear(in_dim, 1)

        self.reset_parameters()

    def reset_parameters(self):
        for lin in self.hidden_layers:
            glorot_uniform_(lin.weight)
            init.zeros_(lin.bias)
        glorot_uniform_(self.output_layer.weight)
        init.zeros_(self.output_layer.bias)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def forward(self, x, dropout=True):
        """Forward pass.

        With ``dropout=True`` the inverted-dropout scaling is applied before
        every weight layer, exactly like Keras' ``Dropout(...)(x, training=True)``.
        This is the stochastic forward pass used both for training and for the
        MC-dropout test-time estimate (R8).
        """
        h = x
        for lin in self.hidden_layers:
            if dropout and self.dropout_p > 0.0:
                h = nn.functional.dropout(h, p=self.dropout_p, training=True)
            h = torch.relu(lin(h))
        if dropout and self.dropout_p > 0.0:
            h = nn.functional.dropout(h, p=self.dropout_p, training=True)
        return self.output_layer(h)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def n_parameters(self):
        return sum(p.numel() for p in self.parameters())

    def weight_sq_sum(self):
        """sum_i ||W_i||^2 over the weight matrices (biases are not decayed)."""
        total = x_new = 0.0
        for lin in list(self.hidden_layers) + [self.output_layer]:
            total = total + (lin.weight ** 2).sum()
        return total


def compute_weight_decay(tau, lengthscale, n_train, dropout):
    """lambda = l^2 * (1 - p) / (2 * N * tau)   -- net/net.py line 72.

    This is the regulariser of paper eq. (4), p_i*l^2/(2*tau*N)*||M_i||^2, with
    p_i the *keep* probability (1 - dropout rate); eq. (7) is the p = 1 case.
    """
    return float(lengthscale ** 2 * (1.0 - dropout) / (2.0 * n_train * tau))

"""Training + MC-dropout evaluation, ported from repo/net/net.py to PyTorch.

Fidelity notes (what the released Keras/Theano code does and what we mirror):

* Objective (Keras 2.2): ``loss = mean_over_batch((y - yhat)^2)
  + reg * sum_layers ||W||^2`` where ``reg = l^2 (1-p) / (2 N tau)`` and N is
  the number of rows of the block being fitted.  The regulariser is NOT scaled
  by the batch size (Keras adds layer losses to the batch-mean data loss).
* Optimiser: Adam, lr 1e-3, betas (0.9, 0.999), eps 1e-8 (Keras defaults).
* Mini-batches of ``batch_size`` with per-epoch shuffling (Keras fit default).
* Fixed number of epochs, no early stopping (R12).
* Prediction: T stochastic forward passes with dropout ON (Keras
  ``Dropout(..., training=True)`` inside ``model.predict``), averaged for the
  predictive mean (eq. 6 / R8); predictive log-likelihood via the log-sum-exp
  Monte-Carlo approximation of eq. (8) as coded in net/net.py (A22).
"""

import math

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

import config
from model import DropoutRegressor, compute_weight_decay


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def train_network(X_train, y_train, n_hidden, dropout, tau, lengthscale,
                  n_epochs, batch_size, lr, seed=None, log_every=None,
                  verbose=False):
    """Fit one dropout network; returns the trained model and its weight decay.

    @param X_train  (N, Q) standardised features
    @param y_train  (N,)   standardised targets
    @param n_hidden list with the number of units per hidden layer
    """
    if seed is not None:
        torch.manual_seed(seed)

    N = X_train.shape[0]
    reg = compute_weight_decay(tau, lengthscale, N, dropout)

    model = DropoutRegressor(X_train.shape[1], n_hidden=n_hidden[0],
                             dropout=dropout,
                             n_hidden_layers=len(n_hidden))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr,
                           betas=config.ADAM_BETAS, eps=config.ADAM_EPS)

    Xt = torch.as_tensor(X_train, dtype=torch.float32)
    yt = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(y_train, dtype=np.float32).ravel(),
                         dtype=torch.float32).view(-1, 1)

    n = Xt.shape[0]
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0 if seed is None else seed)
    model.train()
    for epoch in range(int(n_epochs)):
        perm = torch.randperm(n, generator=generator) if config.SHUFFLE_EPOCHS \
            else torch.arange(n)
        for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[start:start + batch_size]
            opt.zero_grad()
            pred = model(Xt[idx], dropout=True)
            data_loss = ((pred - yt[idx]) ** 2).mean()
            loss = data_loss + reg * model.weight_sq_sum()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
        if verbose and log_every and (epoch + 1) % log_every == 0:
            print("    epoch %4d  loss %.6f" % (epoch + 1, float(loss)))
    model.lambda_ = reg
    return model


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Monte-Carlo dropout prediction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def mc_predict(model, X, T=1000, chunk=None, tau=None):
    """T stochastic forward passes (eq. 6 / R8).

    Returns (mean, var) in the *standardised* target space, plus the raw
    (T, n) sample matrix used for the eq. (8) log-likelihood.
    """
    if chunk is None:
        chunk = config.MC_CHUNK
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    n = X.shape[0]
    Xt = torch.as_tensor(X, dtype=torch.float32)

    was_training = model.training
    model.train()          # dropout stays ON: this is MC dropout
    sums = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.float64)
    sums_sq = np.zeros(n, dtype=np.float64)
    samples = np.zeros((T, n), dtype=np.float64)
    done = 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        while done < T:
            t = min(chunk, T - done)
            # (t, n, Q) -> one big batch; dropout masks are independent per row,
            # which is exactly T independent stochastic forward passes.
            rep = Xt.unsqueeze(0).expand(t, n, Xt.shape[1]).reshape(t * n, -1)
            out = model(rep, dropout=True).view(t, n).numpy().astype(np.float64)
            samples[done:done + t] = out
            sums += out.sum(axis=0)
            sums_sq += (out ** 2).sum(axis=0)
            done += t
    if not was_training:
        model.eval()
    mean = sums / T
    var = sums_sq / T - mean ** 2
    var = np.maximum(var, 0.0)
    return mean, var, samples


def _logsumexp(a, axis=0):
    m = np.max(a, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    m = np.where(np.isfinite(m), m, 0.0)
    out = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(a - m), axis=axis, keepdims=True)) + m
    return out.squeeze(axis=axis)


def evaluate(model, X, y_orig, scaler_y, T=1000, tau=1.0):
    """MC-dropout test RMSE (original units) and predictive log-likelihood.

    Mirrors net/net.py ``predict``: predictions are inverse-transformed with the
    training-target mean/std before the RMSE, and the log-likelihood uses the
    log-sum-exp form of eq. (8) as implemented in the released code (A22).
    """
    y_orig = np.asarray(y_orig, dtype=np.float64).ravel()
    mean_std, var_std, samples_std = mc_predict(model, X, T=T)

    # inverse-transform to the original target units (A13)
    mean = scaler_y.inverse_transform(mean_std)
    samples = scaler_y.inverse_transform(samples_std)

    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_orig - mean) ** 2)))

    # eq. (8) / net.py: logsumexp(-0.5*tau*(y - yhat)^2) - log T
    #                   - 0.5*log(2*pi) + 0.5*log(tau)
    ll_terms = (-0.5 * tau * (y_orig[None, :] - samples) ** 2.0)
    ll = (_logsumexp(ll_terms, axis=0) - math.log(T)
          - 0.5 * math.log(2.0 * math.pi) + 0.5 * math.log(tau))
    test_ll = float(np.mean(ll))

    # single stochastic forward pass (the "standard" estim

"""Reproduce Table 1 (Boston Housing, MC dropout) of
"Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep
Learning" (Gal & Ghahramani, 2015/2016; arXiv:1506.02142).

    python reproduce.py                     # default: bostonHousing, 5 splits
    python reproduce.py --smoke             # tiny data-flow check
    python reproduce.py --split-count 20    # all released splits
    python reproduce.py --dataset yacht     # another UCI dataset

Protocol (authors' released repo/experiment.py + repo/net/net.py, ported to
PyTorch because Keras 2.2 / Theano 0.8.2 cannot be installed on Python 3.12):

  for each released train/test split:
      * carve the training block deterministically into 80% fit / 20% validation
      * grid-search (dropout rate, tau) scored by validation predictive
        log-likelihood  [the authors' 2018 replacement for the paper's
        40-iteration Spearmint BO]
      * retrain on the whole training block with the selected hyper-parameters
        for 10x the 40-epoch base schedule (= 400 epochs), no early stopping
      * evaluate MC-dropout test RMSE (eq. 6) and predictive log-likelihood
        (eq. 8) with T stochastic forward passes
  report mean +/- standard error over the splits.
"""

import argparse
import json
import math
import os
import time

import numpy as np

import config
import data_utils
import mc_dropout

# Paper Table 1, Boston Housing, Dropout column (target of claim C1).
TARGET_RMSE = 2.97
TARGET_SE = 0.19
TOLERANCE = 0.19


def parse_args():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    p.add_argument("--dataset", default=config.DATASET)
    p.add_argument("--split-count", type=int, default=config.DEFAULT_N_SPLITS,
                   help="number of the released splits to average over")
    p.add_argument("--splits", default=None,
                   help="explicit comma separated split list, e.g. 0,1,2")
    p.add_argument("--epoch-multiplier", type=int, default=config.EPOCH_MULTIPLIER)
    p.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=config.BATCH_SIZE)
    p.add_argument("--t-test", type=int, default=config.T_TEST)
    p.add_argument("--t-grid", type=int, default=config.T_GRID)
    p.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=config.SEED)
    p.add_argument("--smoke", action="store_true")
    p.add_argument("--out", default=os.path.join(config.RESULTS_DIR,
                                                 "metrics.json"))
    return p.parse_args()


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    t0 = time.time()

    if args.smoke:
        cfg = dict(config.SMOKE)
        cfg["dataset"] = args.dataset
    else:
        cfg = dict(dataset=args.dataset, n_splits=args.split_count,
                   n_epochs=None, t_test=args.t_test, t_grid=args.t_grid,
                   max_train_rows=None, grid_dropout_rates=None,
                   grid_tau_values=None)

    dataset = cfg["dataset"]
    ds_cfg = data_utils.load_dataset_config(dataset)
    n_epochs = cfg["n_epochs"] or int(ds_cfg["n_epochs"] * args.epoch_multiplier)
    dropout_rates = cfg["grid_dropout_rates"] or ds_cfg["dropout_rates"]
    tau_values = cfg["grid_tau_values"] or ds_cfg["tau_values"]
    n_hidden = [ds_cfg["n_hidden"]] * config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS

    if args.splits:
        splits = [int(s) for s in args.splits.split(",")]
    else:
        splits = list(range(cfg["n_splits"]))

    print("=" * 72)
    print("dataset            : %s" % dataset)
    print("hidden layers      : %s" % n_hidden)
    print("epochs             : %d (base %d x multiplier %d)"
          % (n_epochs, ds_cfg["n_epochs"], args.epoch_multiplier))
    print("batch size         : %d" % args.batch_size)
    print("dropout grid       : %s" % dropout_rates)
    print("tau grid           : %s" % tau_values)
    print("length-scale l     : %g" % config.LENGTHSCALE)
    print("T (test / grid)    : %d / %d" % (cfg["t_test"], cfg["t_grid"]))
    print("splits             : %s" % splits)
    print("=" * 72)

    per_split = []
    for split in splits:
        sd = data_utils.make_split(dataset, split, verbose=True)
        if cfg["max_train_rows"]:
            for k in ("X_fit", "y_fit"):
                sd[k] = sd[k][:cfg["max_train_rows"]]
            sd["n_fit"] = sd["X_fit"].shape[0]

"""Print the authors' released per-split results next to ours.

Usage:  python compare_with_released.py [dataset]
"""

import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

import config
import data_utils


def load_released(dataset):
    p = config.dataset_paths(dataset)
    out = {}
    for name in ("test_MC_rmse", "test_rmse", "test_ll", "test_tau"):
        for mult in (100, 10, 500):
            f = os.path.join(p["results_dir"],
                             "%s_%d_xepochs_%d_hidden_layers.txt"
                             % (name, mult, config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS))
            if os.path.exists(f):
                out[name] = dict(multiplier=mult,
                                 values=[float(x) for x in open(f).read().split()])
                break
    return out


def main():
    dataset = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else config.DATASET
    rel = load_released(dataset)
    ours = None
    path = os.path.join(config.RESULTS_DIR, "metrics.json")
    if os.path.exists(path):
        ours = json.load(open(path))

    print("dataset: %s" % dataset)
    for name, d in rel.items():
        v = np.array(d["values"])
        print("  released %-12s (%d_xepochs = %d epochs): mean %.4f  se %.4f  "
              "n=%d" % (name, d["multiplier"],
                        int(np.loadtxt(config.dataset_paths(dataset)["n_epochs"]))
                        * d["multiplier"], v.mean(),
                        v.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(v)), len(v)))
        print("    per-split: " + " ".join("%.4f" % x for x in v))

    if ours and ours.get("dataset") == dataset:
        print("\n  ours (%d splits): mean %.4f  se %.4f"
              % (len(ours["per_split"]), ours["value"],
                 ours.get("std_error", float("nan"))))
        print("    per-split: " + " ".join(
            "%.4f" % r["rmse"] for r in ours["per_split"]))
        if "test_MC_rmse" in rel:
            rv = rel["test_MC_rmse"]["values"]
            print("\n  split-by-split (released vs ours):")

"""Print the authors' released per-split results next to ours.

Usage:  python compare_with_released.py [dataset]
"""

import json
import os
import sys

import numpy as np

import config
import data_utils


def load_released(dataset):
    p = config.dataset_paths(dataset)
    out = {}
    for name in ("test_MC_rmse", "test_rmse", "test_ll", "test_tau"):
        for mult in (100, 10, 500):
            f = os.path.join(p["results_dir"],
                             "%s_%d_xepochs_%d_hidden_layers.txt"
                             % (name, mult, config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS))
            if os.path.exists(f):
                out[name] = dict(multiplier=mult,
                                 values=[float(x) for x in open(f).read().split()])
                break
    return out


def main():
    dataset = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else config.DATASET
    rel = load_released(dataset)
    ours = None
    path = os.path.join(config.RESULTS_DIR, "metrics.json")
    if os.path.exists(path):
        ours = json.load(open(path))

    print("dataset: %s" % dataset)
    for name, d in rel.items():
        v = np.array(d["values"])
        n_ep = int(np.loadtxt(config.dataset_paths(dataset)["n_epochs"]))
        print("  released %-12s (%d_xepochs = %d epochs): mean %.4f  se %.4f  n=%d"
              % (name, d["multiplier"], n_ep * d["multiplier"], v.mean(),
                 v.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(v)), len(v)))
        print("    per-split: " + " ".join("%.4f" % x for x in v))

    if ours and ours.get("dataset") == dataset:
        print("\n  ours (%d splits): mean %.4f" % (len(ours["per_split"]),
                                                   ours["value"]))
        print("    per-split: " + " ".join(
            "%.4f" % r["rmse"] for r in ours["per_split"]))
        if "test_MC_rmse" in rel:
            rv = rel["test_MC_rmse"]["values"]
            print("\n  split-by-split (released vs ours):")
            for i, r in enumerate(ours["per_split"]):
                if i < len(rv):
                    print("    split %2d: released %8.4f   ours %8.4f   diff %+7.4f"
                          % (r["split"], rv[i], r["rmse"], r["rmse"] - rv[i]))
    else:
        print("\n  (no results/metrics.json for this dataset yet)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def train_network(X_train, y_train, n_hidden, dropout, tau, lengthscale,
                  n_epochs, batch_size, lr, log_every=None, verbose=False):
    """Fit one dropout network; returns the trained model and its weight decay.

    The global torch RNG is seeded once per split by the caller (as the released
    code leaves the initialisation to the backend RNG), so every model in the
    grid search gets its own random Glorot initialisation, like the original.

    @param X_train  (N, Q) standardised features
    @param y_train  (N,)   standardised targets
    @param n_hidden list with the number of units per hidden layer
    """
    N = X_train.shape[0]
    reg = compute_weight_decay(tau, lengthscale, N, dropout)

    model = DropoutRegressor(X_train.shape[1], n_hidden=n_hidden[0],
                             dropout=dropout,
                             n_hidden_layers=len(n_hidden))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr,
                           betas=config.ADAM_BETAS, eps=config.ADAM_EPS)

def _grid_job(job):
    """Train one (dropout, tau) candidate and score it on the validation block.

    Module-level so it can be pickled for a multiprocessing pool.  Each job
    seeds the RNG deterministically from its grid index, so the result does not
    depend on the scheduling order.
    """
    (X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val_orig, scaler_y, n_hidden, dropout, tau,
     lengthscale, n_epochs, batch_size, lr, T, seed) = job
    torch.set_num_threads(1)          # one core per worker, no oversubscription
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = train_network(X_fit, y_fit, n_hidden, dropout, tau, lengthscale,
                          n_epochs, batch_size, lr)
    res = evaluate(model, X_val, y_val_orig, scaler_y, T=T, tau=tau)
    return dict(dropout=dropout, tau=tau, ll=res["ll"], rmse=res["rmse"])


def grid_search(X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val_orig, scaler_y, dropout_rates,
                tau_values, n_hidden, lengthscale, n_epochs, batch_size, lr,
                T=None, seed=0, n_jobs=1, verbose=False):
    """Select (dropout, tau) by validation predictive log-likelihood.

    The 12 candidates of the released grid are independent fits, so they are
    farmed out to a process pool when ``n_jobs > 1`` (pure speed-up: identical
    protocol, identical per-job seeds).
    """
    if T is None:
        T = config.T_GRID
    jobs = []
    i = 0
    for dropout in dropout_rates:
        for tau in tau_values:
            jobs.append((X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val_orig, scaler_y, n_hidden,
                         dropout, tau, lengthscale, n_epochs, batch_size, lr,
                         T, int(seed) + 1000 * i))
            i += 1

    history = None
    if n_jobs > 1 and len(jobs) > 1:
        try:
            import multiprocessing as mp
            ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")
            with ctx.Pool(processes=min(n_jobs, len(jobs))) as pool:
                history = pool.map(_grid_job, jobs)
        except Exception as exc:            # pragma: no cover - safety net
            print("    parallel grid search unavailable (%s); "
                  "running sequentially" % exc)
            history = None
    if history is None:
        history = [_grid_job(j) for j in jobs]

    best = dict(ll=-float("inf"), dropout=None, tau=None)
    for row in history:
        if verbose:
            print("    grid dropout=%-6g tau=%-6g  val_ll=%9.4f  val_rmse=%7.4f"
                  % (row["dropout"], row["tau"], row["ll"], row["rmse"]))
        if row["ll"] > best["ll"]:
            best = dict(ll=row["ll"], dropout=row["dropout"], tau=row["tau"])
    best["history"] = history
    return best

def _notes(n, n_splits_total, n_epochs, batch_size, t_test):
    if n >= n_splits_total:
        head = ("Full averaging protocol: all %d released random splits were "
                "used, as in the paper (R10)." % n)
    else:
        head = ("Scale-down: %d of the %d released random splits were averaged "
                "(paper R10 uses %d), so the standard error is ~sqrt(%d/%d)=%.2fx "
                "wider than the paper's."
                % (n, n_splits_total, n_splits_total, n_splits_total, n,
                   math.sqrt(n_splits_total / float(n))))

            "dropout before every weight layer, same released dropout/tau "

target.statement: MC dropout test RMSE on Boston Housing is 2.97 ± 0.19 (mean ± standard error over 20 random splits), outperforming PBP (3.01 ± 0.18) and VI (4.32 ± 0.29).
target.table_ref: Table 1, row Boston Housing, column Dropout (Avg. Test RMSE and Std. Errors)

tolerance.why: Table 1 reports ±0.19 standard error over 20 random splits for Boston Housing RMSE in the target Dropout configuration; this is the paper's reported spread for the target setting.

audit_summary: The run is a faithful port of the authors' released experiment.py/net.py protocol: 1x50 ReLU net with dropout before every weight layer, lambda = l^2(1-p)/(2N tau) with l=1e-2, 400 epochs (10x the 40-epoch base), Adam with batch 32, no early stopping, T=10000 MC-dropout passes, and all 20 released Boston Housing 90/10 splits with the released standardisation - i.e. the C1 contract's configuration on every axis that defines the number. It reports 3.1171 +- 0.2024 test RMSE (LL -2.5188 +- 0.0599), 0.147 above the paper's 2.97 +- 0.19 and inside the +-0.19 tolerance, with a standard error close to the paper's. Anti-cheat is clean: the metric is test RMSE in original units computed from the run's own per-split predictions, the grid search selects on validation log-likelihood only (no test contamination), and TARGET_RMSE=2.97 in reproduce.py appears solely in the tolerance comparison, not in any reported value. The only protocol deviations are the hyper-parameter search (authors' 2018 12-candidate released grid instead of 40-iteration Spearmint BO), the PyTorch framework, a single dropout rate per model instead of the paper's two, and batch 32 (paper) vs 128 (released net.py) - all disclosed in config.py, A16-A24 and the metrics notes. Nothing was scaled down: the router's 5-split contingency was abandoned (A23), and the clean 589.6 s re-run used all 20 splits, the full 400-epoch schedule and T=10000, so the reported mean/SE are directly comparable to the paper's. Residual gap is dominated by the paper's underspecification and seed-level randomness, and note the A15 ambiguity that the shipped 4000-epoch files give 2.9036, nearer Table 1's 2.97 than Table 2's 2.80.

requirement_check.evidence: config.N_HIDDEN_LAYERS=1 and n_hidden=50 read from the released n_hidden.txt; model.DropoutRegressor builds 13->50->1 (checks.py asserts 751 parameters); per_split rows show Q=13 and the 1x50 net for every one of the 20 splits.

Dropout is applied before every weight layer (model.forward), satisfying R2's structure, but a single rate per split drawn from the authors' released grid {0.005,0.01,0.05,0.1} is used (selected 0.005 x2, 0.01 x5, 0.05 x8, 0.1 x5), not the paper's two probabilities 0.05 and 0.005 at different layers (A2). 0.1 is outside the paper's stated pair; config.py/A2 justify this from the released net/net.py, which also uses one rate per layer.

compute_weight_decay implements lambda = l^2*(1-p)/(2*N*tau) and the training loss adds reg*sum||W||^2 (biases excluded), i.e. L2 weight decay derived from tau and l. The algebraic form follows the authors' released net/net.py rather than the reader's eq.(7) reading; the discrepancy is recorded and risk-flagged in A20 and the metrics config string.

The 40-iteration Spearmint BO was not reproduced; hyper-parameters are chosen by an exhaustive 12-candidate grid over the released dropout_rates.txt x tau_values.txt scored by validation predictive log-likelihood (A18/A24), parallelised over 7 workers (verified identical selection to the sequential run). Same selection criterion (validation LL), different search procedure; disclosed in config.py, reproduce.py notes and A18/A24.

n_epochs = 40 (n_epochs.txt) x multiplier 10 = 400; metrics.config records n_epochs=400, n_epochs_base=40, epoch_multiplier=10. The clean re-run used the default multiplier (no --epoch-multiplier override).
batch_size=32 (paper text) and Adam with lr=1e-3, betas (0.9,0.999), eps 1e-8; the released net/net.py hard-codes 128, and the 32-vs-128 deviation is explicitly recorded in A16 and the metrics notes.
config.LENGTHSCALE = 1e-2, threaded through train_network/compute_weight_decay and printed in the run header and metrics.config prior_length_scale=0.01.

mc_dropout.mc_predict keeps the model in train mode and performs T=10000 independent stochastic forward passes (chunked), returning the mean used for the test RMSE after inverse-transforming to original target units (evaluate()).

evaluate() computes the eq.(8) Monte-Carlo predictive log-likelihood via logsumexp(-0.5*tau*(y-yhat)^2) - log T - 0.5 log 2pi + 0.5 log tau (net/net.py form, A22); it drives the validation-based grid selection and yields mean test LL -2.5188 +- 0.0599.

All 20 released splits were used (A23 supersedes A19's 5-split plan); metrics.json split field says '20 of the 20 released random splits', the clean re-run tail shows splits up to 19, and the mean/SE are over n=20 with ddof=1.

Uses the released UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing data (506 rows, index_features/index_target, index_train_i/index_test_i, 455/51 per split) and net.py-standardisation of inputs and targets fitted on the trained block; checks.py verifies split disjointness/coverage and the 20% validation carve used by the authors' experiment.py (A17).
config.EARLY_STOPPING=False; training runs exactly int(n_epochs)=400 epochs with no validation-based stopping or LR decay (mc_dropout.train_network).

Implemented in PyTorch 2.14.0+cpu (CPU) rather than Keras 2.2 / Theano 0.8.2, which cannot be installed on Python 3.12; Keras 2.2 semantics are reproduced (Glorot-uniform kernels, zero biases, L2 on kernels only, inverted dropout, Adam defaults, batch-mean MSE). Recorded in R13 of the metrics notes and A16/A17; a framework port, not a change of method.
